topic: Pilot sample that does not represent production intake
stem: A bank piloted a Claude-based small-business loan-document checker on 1,200 applications hand-picked by the pilot lead as representative, reaching 93% accuracy. Production intake includes 18% of applications submitted as phone-camera photographs of paper forms; the pilot set contained none, because the pilot lead excluded them as not a fair test. The lead also chose which applications to include in every other category. What should the architect insist on before production?

options.text: Proceed with the 93% figure and monitor accuracy closely in production, since photographed applications are a minority of intake and any problem will surface in the first weeks.
Proceed, adding a preprocessing step that diverts photographed applications into a manual queue so the checker only ever sees the kind of input it was measured on.
Re-measure on a random sample of real intake, photographs included, and set the production expectation from that number.
Run a second pilot on 1,200 photographed applications to obtain a segment-specific figure, then combine the two results weighted by volume share.

explanation.correct: The 93% describes a population that does not exist in production. The photographs are the visible part of the problem; the sentence that matters is that the lead chose every case, so selection bias is present across all categories and its direction is unknown. Only a randomly drawn sample of real intake produces a number that can be quoted as the production expectation, and it also produces the baseline against which post-launch monitoring will be interpreted. Without it, every future quality reading has nothing to be compared with.

distractors.A: Monitoring in production only tells you something if you know what to expect; here the expectation is derived from a biased sample. It also accepts an unknown accuracy on nearly a fifth of real volume before anyone has looked at it.
distractors.B: Routing 18% of intake to manual handling is a substantial operational commitment nobody has planned or staffed, and it is being made to protect a measurement rather than because photographs cannot be processed. Nobody has yet checked whether the checker handles them.
distractors.D: This fixes the photograph gap and leaves the hand-picking untouched, so the 82% segment figure remains unreliable. A volume-weighted combination of one biased number and one clean number is still biased.

explanation.concept: A pilot's accuracy figure is a claim about a population, and it is only valid for the population the sample was drawn from. Sample randomly from real intake, including the awkward inputs the pilot lead wanted to exclude — the awkward inputs are usually where the system fails and always where the production number comes from.
explanation.tip: Look for who chose the sample. Hand-picked, curated or representative-by-judgement all mean the same thing, and the correct response is to redraw the sample rather than to patch the specific exclusion the stem names.

topic: Handover pack contrasted with the runbook
stem: In an ownership transfer to a run team, what distinguishes the handover pack from the runbook?

options.text: The handover pack is authored by the build team, whereas the runbook is authored by the receiving run team once it has operated the system long enough to know what breaks.
The runbook holds procedures executed during an incident; the handover pack holds the context needed to make changes over the system's life.
The handover pack is a permanent record for audit, while the runbook is discarded once the run team is confident operating the system.
The runbook covers the application layer while the handover pack covers infrastructure, credentials and cloud accounts.

explanation.correct: The two documents are separated by the reader's situation. A runbook is read under pressure by someone who needs to act, so it is short, procedural, and organised by symptom. A handover pack is read at leisure by someone deciding whether a change is safe, so it carries design rationale, dependency maps, evaluation approach, cost model and known limitations. Mixing them makes the runbook too long to use in an incident and buries the design context nobody has time to search for.

distractors.A: Both are normally drafted by the build team and corrected by the run team as it gains experience. Authorship does not distinguish them, and a runbook that only exists after the first incident has failed its purpose.
distractors.C: Neither is disposable. Runbooks are living documents that grow an entry per new failure signature, and confidence is exactly when people stop remembering the rare procedures. An AI system's runbook in particular grows an entry every time a new production failure signature appears.
distractors.D: The split is by reading situation, not by layer. A runbook covers infrastructure actions such as failover, and a handover pack covers application design. Both documents span every layer; only the reading situation separates them.

explanation.concept: Split operational documentation by when it is read. Incident-time material is procedural, symptom-indexed and short; change-time material is explanatory, decision-oriented and can be long. For an AI system the runbook must include prompt and model rollback, and the handover pack must include the evaluation approach and known failure modes.
explanation.tip: Ask which document the on-call engineer opens at three in the morning. Anything that would not be opened then belongs in the other one, regardless of how important it is.

topic: Evidence supporting promotion from pilot to production
stem: A grocery wholesaler's pilot of a Claude-based invoice-discrepancy assistant has ended and the steering group must decide on promotion to production. Which of the following, if true, constitute evidence that it should be promoted? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: The accuracy threshold agreed before the pilot was met on a sample drawn randomly from real invoice intake.
Users rated the assistant highly in the post-pilot satisfaction survey, with most saying they would like to keep it.
The assistant's p95 latency sat comfortably inside the internal target throughout, measured on pilot traffic at a tenth of production volume.
The measured benefit exceeds the fully loaded run cost, including the human review time the workflow requires.
A named team has accepted operational ownership, with an on-call rotation and the authority to roll back.

explanation.correct: Promotion needs three independent things to be true: the system works on the real population, the economics are positive once you count everything, and someone can run it. The accuracy result matters because the sample was random and the threshold was pre-agreed. The benefit figure matters because it is net of human review, which is where assistive systems quietly lose their case. Accepted ownership with rollback authority matters because a system with no operator is not production-ready however good its numbers are.

distractors.B: Satisfaction tells you people are willing, which is worth knowing for adoption planning. It is not evidence of value or of correctness, and it is the signal a fluent but unreliable assistant scores best on.
distractors.C: Latency measured at a tenth of production volume says nothing about latency at full volume, so this is not yet evidence of anything. Re-measure under representative load before treating it as a passed criterion.

explanation.concept: A promotion decision rests on three legs: proven benefit against a pre-agreed threshold on a representative sample, positive economics fully loaded, and an accountable operator with rollback authority. Missing any one of them is a hold. Sentiment and unscaled performance figures feel supportive and carry no weight.
explanation.tip: Check what each figure was measured on. A number taken at a tenth of production volume, or from a curated sample, is not a smaller version of the real number — it is a different number.

topic: Rollout pace when expert users are being deskilled
stem: A specialist translation agency introduced a Claude-based first-draft translator; its thirty senior linguists now post-edit rather than translate. Over four months, throughput rose 40%, three of the five most productive linguists resigned citing loss of craft, and the agency's independent quality audit score fell from 4.6 to 4.1 out of 5. The chief operating officer wants to accelerate the rollout to the remaining teams. What should the architect advise?

options.text: Pause the rollout and redesign the role so linguists retain original translation work on the content types where the audit score fell, before extending it further.
Accelerate as planned, since a 40% throughput gain is a larger and more durable commercial effect than a half-point movement on an internal five-point audit scale that customers never see.
Introduce a retention bonus for senior linguists, targeted at the individuals whose output the audit scores depend on most.
Move to a higher-capability model tier so first drafts require less post-editing, removing the repetitive work the linguists object to.

explanation.correct: Two signals point the same way and they are connected: the people who produced the quality are leaving, and the quality has fallen. Extending a role design that drives out senior practitioners multiplies the problem across the remaining teams, and the capability being lost cannot be rehired quickly. Redesigning so that senior linguists keep original work — particularly on the content where the audit dropped — addresses both the attrition cause and the quality gap, and it can be evaluated before the rollout continues.

distractors.B: Throughput and quality are being traded, and the trade has not been priced. A specialist agency sells audited quality, so a half-point fall on its own audit scale is a movement in the thing customers buy, not an internal metric to be discounted.
distractors.C: A bonus pays people to stay in a role they have said they do not want. It may slow the attrition, and it does nothing about the quality drop or about the design flaw that produced both.
distractors.D: Less post-editing means even less craft, which accelerates the cause the resignations named. It also reduces the human contribution to quality precisely when the audit says quality is falling. It also spends money on the assumption that the objection was to effort rather than to the shape of the work.

explanation.concept: When automation converts skilled creation into review, treat role design as part of the system design. Watch attrition among top performers and independent quality measures together: rising throughput alongside falling quality and senior departures is a signal the operating model is wrong, not a signal to scale it faster.
explanation.tip: When a stem pairs a productivity gain with both a quality drop and the departure of the best people, the productivity number is the distractor. Ask what the organisation actually sells.

topic: Shipping a breaking output change to internal consumers
stem: An internal platform team owns a Claude-based entity-extraction service used by four applications. A prompt change improves extraction recall but also changes date fields from free text to ISO-8601. Two of the four consumers parse dates with regular expressions tuned to the current format and will break. How should the change be shipped?

options.text: Ship to all four consumers with a release note; ISO-8601 is unambiguously the better format, and updating a regular expression is a small change each team can absorb inside a sprint.
Add a permanent compatibility layer that renders ISO dates back into the current free-text format, so no consumer ever has to change.
Version the endpoint and keep both versions running indefinitely, so each consumer migrates only if and when it chooses to.
Ship behind a per-consumer flag defaulting to current behaviour, with a dated cutover once both affected consumers confirm they have migrated.

explanation.correct: The recall improvement and the format change are bundled in one prompt change but affect consumers differently, so the flag lets the two unaffected applications take the benefit immediately while the two that would break stay on current behaviour until they are ready. The default matters: defaulting to the old behaviour means nobody breaks through inaction. The date matters equally, because a flag without a cutover date becomes a permanent fork that the platform team maintains forever.

distractors.A: The change is trivial for the platform team and lands in someone else's sprint. Breaking two internal consumers without their agreement is how a shared platform loses the trust that makes it shared.
distractors.B: A permanent translation layer preserves a format nobody wants and hides the improvement from consumers who would benefit from ISO dates. It also becomes untouchable code, since removing it later is the same breaking change deferred.
distractors.C: Indefinite dual versions double the surface the platform team tests and evaluates on every subsequent prompt change. Versioned endpoints are reasonable; the missing element is an end date. Keep the versioned surface if it helps, and attach a published expiry date to the old one.

explanation.concept: For a breaking change to internal consumers, ship the new behaviour behind a per-consumer switch that defaults to the old behaviour, and pair it with a published cutover date. Opt-in protects consumers from your schedule; the date protects you from maintaining two behaviours forever.
explanation.tip: Options offering unlimited backwards compatibility are almost always wrong on this exam. The correct shape is nearly always a temporary compatibility path with a published expiry.

topic: Live configuration that has drifted from source control
stem: During a routine review, the run team at a freight forwarder finds that the live system prompt in the configuration store differs from the version in the Git repository. The store's audit log shows an edit made three weeks ago from a developer's account, outside the deployment pipeline. Quality metrics have been stable throughout the three weeks, and the current live prompt has never been through the evaluation gate. What is the next step?

options.text: Capture the live prompt as a new versioned commit through the normal pipeline, then close the direct-write path so only the pipeline can change the store.
Revert the store to the repository version immediately, since the live prompt is unreviewed and source control must be the authority.
Open a disciplinary process against the developer whose account made the out-of-band change before altering anything in the environment.
Add a nightly reconciliation job that alerts the run team whenever the store and the repository diverge, and take the finding to the next iteration planning session for a decision.

explanation.correct: Three weeks of stable metrics say the live prompt is the behaviour the business currently has and is not causing harm, so the urgent problem is not the prompt — it is that production is running a configuration nobody can reproduce and the store can be written to outside the pipeline. Committing the live text and running it through the gate makes the current state reproducible and evaluated without changing behaviour. Closing the direct-write path stops the next occurrence, which detection alone would not.

distractors.B: Reverting is itself an unevaluated behaviour change, made blind, on a system that is currently stable. Source control is the authority in principle, and restoring it by pushing an untested change into production inverts the risk you are trying to reduce.
distractors.C: Whether the change was reckless is a conversation for afterwards, and it is usually a process gap rather than an individual one. Meanwhile production still runs an unreproducible configuration and the write path is still open.
distractors.D: Detection is useful and belongs in the plan, but an alert on divergence is a way of noticing the same problem faster next time. It neither makes the current configuration reproducible nor removes the ability to bypass the pipeline.

explanation.concept: When live configuration has drifted from source control and is behaving acceptably, adopt the live state into version control rather than reverting to the repository. Then close the bypass. Reverting to reclaim tidiness pushes an unevaluated change into a stable system, which is the opposite of what configuration discipline exists to prevent.
explanation.tip: The stable-metrics detail is the discriminator. It converts the live prompt from a suspected fault into the current known-good state, which flips the correct direction of reconciliation.

topic: Question unique to a post-implementation review
stem: What question should a post-implementation review answer that neither the pilot gate nor the production readiness review could?

options.text: Whether the system meets its latency and availability objectives at full production volume.
Whether the benefit forecast at the pilot gate actually materialised at scale, measured the way it was measured then.
Whether the architecture chosen was the best option available at the time the decision was taken, and what the team would choose if it were starting again today.
Whether the delivery team followed the organisation's project methodology and governance steps.

explanation.correct: The pilot gate forecast a benefit from a small, controlled sample; the readiness review asked whether the organisation could operate the thing. Neither can tell you what actually happened once the whole population used it under real conditions, with real adoption rates, real override behaviour and real edge cases. That comparison — forecast against realised, using the same measurement method so the two are comparable — is the post-implementation review's distinctive job and the input that should reshape the roadmap.

distractors.A: Performance against objectives is monitored continuously and does not need a review meeting to surface. It is also something the readiness review already required evidence for. A review that spends its time on availability charts has not used the ninety days of data it was convened to read.
distractors.C: Retrospective architecture debate is worth having occasionally and rarely changes anything, because the decision context has moved. It also tends to consume the meeting that should be reading benefit data.
distractors.D: Methodology compliance is an assurance question owned elsewhere in the organisation, and a project can follow every governance step faultlessly while delivering nothing. It says nothing about whether the system produced the benefit it promised.

explanation.concept: Hold a post-implementation review at a fixed interval after launch and make its central question the comparison of forecast benefit against realised benefit, measured identically. Its outputs are a corrected benefit figure for future business cases and a reprioritised backlog, not a retrospective on how the project was run.
explanation.tip: Each lifecycle gate answers exactly one question the others cannot: pilot asks is the value real, readiness asks can we run it, post-implementation asks did the value arrive. Match the option to the gate.

topic: Sequencing a regulatory change against a benefit change
stem: A payments firm's Claude-based sanctions-narrative assistant faces two competing demands. A regulator's thematic review requires that from 1 March, fourteen weeks away, every automated narrative cites the underlying rule applied. Separately, the operations team wants narratives shortened by 30%, which analysts estimate saves 900 analyst-hours a year. The team can absorb one substantial change per quarter. What should be scheduled first?

options.text: The length reduction, since 900 analyst-hours a year is a quantified recurring benefit and adding a rule citation is a formatting change that can be slotted in at short notice.
Neither yet; approach the supervisor for an extension so the team can sequence both changes against its own quality and release timeline.
The rule citation, because the date is externally set and missing it is a supervisory finding, while the length reduction carries no deadline.
Both in one release, since the citation lengthens narratives and the reduction offsets it, and a single release carries less change risk than two.

explanation.correct: Fourteen weeks is roughly the one change the team can absorb, so the sequencing question is really which item takes the quarter. One has an externally fixed date whose miss produces a supervisory finding; the other has a recurring benefit and no date at all. Deferring the benefit costs a known quantity of analyst time for one quarter; deferring the obligation costs a regulatory outcome the firm does not control. That asymmetry decides it, and the length reduction is not lost — it simply takes the following quarter.

distractors.A: Calling the citation a formatting change underestimates it: the assistant must identify which rule was applied, which is a behaviour change requiring evaluation, not a template edit. The benefit is real and it has no deadline attached.
distractors.B: Requesting an extension on a thematic review deadline spends supervisory goodwill to buy scheduling convenience, and the request may well be refused, leaving the team fourteen weeks minus however long the answer takes.
distractors.D: Bundling a mandatory change with a discretionary one means a problem in either delays both, and the deadline is on the half you cannot slip. It also makes the release's effect on narrative quality harder to attribute.

explanation.concept: Prioritise against constraint type, not benefit size. Externally imposed dated obligations occupy the slot they need; undated benefits, however well quantified, are schedulable. Never bundle a discretionary change into the release carrying a mandatory one, because the bundle inherits the risk of both and the deadline of the strictest.
explanation.tip: Sort backlog items into dated and undated before comparing their value. A large undated benefit loses to a small dated obligation every time the calendar is tight.

topic: What pinning a model version buys and obliges
stem: What does pinning a specific model version in a production system buy, and what obligation does it create?

options.text: It buys a lower and more predictable unit cost on inference, and obliges the team to renegotiate commercial terms at each contract renewal cycle.
It buys higher sustained throughput, and obliges the team to reserve capacity ahead of seasonal peaks.
It buys permanent immunity from provider-side behaviour changes, and creates no continuing obligation.
It buys reproducible behaviour across deployments, and obliges the team to plan and test a migration before that version retires.

explanation.correct: Pinning removes one source of unexplained behaviour change, so a quality movement in production can be attributed to something you did rather than to the model shifting under you. That is what makes evaluation results durable and rollback meaningful. The price is that pinned versions do not last forever, so pinning converts an ambient risk into a scheduled project: track the retirement horizon, diff the successor on your own traffic, and migrate deliberately rather than discovering the deadline late.

distractors.A: Version pinning is a behavioural control, not a commercial one. It does not change unit economics, and commercial renewal is a separate track entirely. Teams sometimes pin for budget predictability, and that is an effect of a contract rather than of the pin.
distractors.B: Throughput is governed by rate limits, concurrency design and capacity arrangements. Choosing a fixed version does not alter how much traffic you can push through it. A pinned version and its successor sit under the same account-level constraints either way.
distractors.C: The immunity is real and it is temporary, which is exactly the point. Treating it as permanent is how teams end up migrating in a hurry against someone else's timetable.

explanation.concept: Pin model versions in production for reproducibility, and treat every pin as a dated liability. Maintain awareness of the retirement horizon for each pinned version, keep a migration evaluation ready, and budget the migration as planned work rather than as an interruption.
explanation.tip: Whenever a question offers a benefit with no cost attached, that option is usually wrong. Pinning is a trade, and the exam wants you to name both halves of it.

topic: Composing the first ring of a phased rollout
stem: A pharmacy-benefits manager is planning ring one of a Claude-based prior-authorisation assistant that will eventually cover 4,000 users across nine regions. The programme has agreed a quality threshold that ring one must clear before ring two opens. Which two properties should ring one have? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: It should consist entirely of volunteers, so that ring-one adoption rates predict adoption in the later rings.
It should include the region with the most atypical case mix, not only the most cooperative region.
It should be confined to a single region so the rollout can be described as geographically contained in board reporting.
It should exclude any region whose case mix differs from the national average, so that ring-one results are clean.
It should be large enough that the agreed quality threshold can actually be evaluated on the traffic it generates.

explanation.correct: A ring has to be both hard enough and big enough. Including an atypical case mix means the ring exercises the inputs likely to break the assistant, which is the point of going first; a ring of easy cases produces a pass that predicts nothing about ring two. Sizing to the threshold is the other half: if the ring cannot generate enough traffic to evaluate the agreed criterion with any precision, the gate cannot be decided and the rollout proceeds on impression.

distractors.A: Volunteers are self-selected enthusiasts, so their adoption rate systematically overstates what the general population will do. They are useful for early feedback and useless as a predictor of anything. Ring one is a measurement, and a self-selected sample cannot support one.
distractors.C: How the rollout is described in board reporting is not a design property. Geographic containment may be convenient, and it does nothing about whether the ring is representative or statistically adequate.
distractors.D: This deliberately removes the cases most likely to reveal problems, producing a clean result that transfers to nothing. It is the same error as curating a pilot sample, applied to a rollout ring.

explanation.concept: Design ring one to be representative-plus-adversarial and statistically sufficient: include the population segments most likely to expose failure, and size it so the ring's own traffic can decide the exit criterion. A comfortable first ring buys confidence without buying information.
explanation.tip: Two failure shapes recur in ring design: too easy, and too small to measure. Options about optics, volunteers or clean samples are always addressing something other than those two.

topic: Preserving the manual fallback capability after automation
stem: An airline moved passenger re-accommodation during irregular operations onto a Claude-based assistant eighteen months ago. During a recent 40-minute outage, the duty team's manual re-accommodation rate ran at about a third of the pre-automation rate, and two of the four duty managers had never performed the task without the assistant. The head of operations wants this addressed before the winter disruption season. What is the right response?

options.text: Schedule regular periods in which duty managers handle re-accommodation manually on live low-severity disruptions, and make demonstrated manual competence a condition of holding the duty rota.
Deploy the assistant across multiple regions to raise its availability, so outages become rare enough that the manual path effectively never has to carry load.
Document the manual procedure in full detail and require every duty manager to read and acknowledge it annually before the season starts.
Build a degraded mode in which a cheaper model tier serves re-accommodation decisions whenever the primary path is unavailable.

explanation.correct: The capability that decayed is human skill, and skill is restored only by practice. Rostering deliberate manual work on low-severity disruptions keeps the fallback exercised at low cost and reveals whether the manual procedure still matches the current systems, which after eighteen months it probably does not. Tying the rota to demonstrated competence makes the practice happen when the season gets busy, which is precisely when a voluntary scheme collapses and when the fallback is most likely to be needed.

distractors.B: Higher availability lowers the probability of the event and leaves its consequence untouched. Winter disruption is exactly when both the assistant and its infrastructure are under most strain, so the residual outage is correlated with the worst possible moment.
distractors.C: Reading a procedure once a year produces acknowledgement, not capability. Two duty managers have never done the task at all, and no document converts that into performance under a live disruption.
distractors.D: A secondary model path is worth having and is not a fallback from the model path failing; it shares dependencies and it still leaves nobody able to act if both are unavailable. It also further removes the humans from the task.

explanation.concept: Automating a task erodes the human capability to perform it, so the manual fallback degrades silently from the day you launch. If a degraded mode depends on people doing the work by hand, that mode must be exercised on a schedule and its competence measured, or it exists only on the diagram.
explanation.tip: When a stem quantifies how badly humans performed during an outage, the question is about skill decay, not availability. Options that make the outage rarer are answering a different question.

stem: After training users to review the output of an AI assistant, which measurement best indicates that the enablement was effective?

options.text: The proportion of trained users who pass the end-of-session knowledge assessment.
The rate at which trained users correctly reject or amend incorrect output on seeded cases.
Weekly active usage among trained users compared against an untrained control group.
Self-reported confidence in reviewing assistant output, collected from users immediately after each session and again a month later.

explanation.correct: The purpose of training a reviewer is to raise their detection rate on wrong output, so measure that directly by seeding known-bad cases into their real queue and observing what they do. It is behavioural, it happens in the working context rather than in a classroom, and it produces a number that can be tracked over time and re-measured when it decays. Every other candidate measures exposure, willingness or belief, none of which predicts whether a bad output gets caught.

distractors.A: Assessment pass rates measure recall of what was said in the session. They correlate weakly with behaviour under time pressure and tend to sit near 100% because the assessment was written by the trainer.
distractors.C: Usage tells you the tool is being adopted, which is a goal in its own right. It is silent on whether the users are catching errors, and rising usage with unchanged detection is the automation-bias failure.
distractors.D: Confidence measured immediately after training reliably rises and is the one indicator you should distrust most, since overconfident reviewers approve faster. Collect it as a check on whether the session was tolerable, never as evidence that detection improved.

explanation.concept: Measure enablement by behaviour change in the real workflow, not by completion, satisfaction or confidence. For review roles the measurable behaviour is detection: seed known-bad cases, observe the catch rate, and re-measure periodically because the skill decays as the system's output improves.
explanation.tip: Rank training metrics by how close they sit to the outcome you want. Attendance, assessment, confidence and usage are all proxies for a proxy; catch rate on seeded errors is the thing itself.

topic: Choosing the axis for phasing a multi-site rollout
stem: A multinational manufacturer is rolling out a Claude-based safety-incident report assistant across 22 sites in six countries. It can phase by site — every incident type at one site, then the next — or by incident type — one type across all sites, then the next. The prompt and the retrieval index are built per incident type; site differences amount to interface language and a few local reporting fields, both handled through configuration. Which phasing should it choose?

options.text: Phase by site, so each phase sits inside a single management chain and the change can be led locally by that site's leadership.
Phase by region, grouping sites by time zone so that support coverage can follow the rollout around the clock.
Phase by incident type across all sites, so each phase validates one prompt-and-index artefact end to end.
Phase by incident type, but only at English-language sites first, deferring all localisation to a separate later programme.

explanation.correct: Phase boundaries should follow the boundaries of the thing that can be wrong. Here the artefacts that carry quality risk are per incident type — one prompt, one index each — while the site dimension is configuration the stem says is already handled. Phasing by incident type means each phase exercises one artefact against the full diversity of sites and can be evaluated, fixed or rolled back as a unit. Phasing by site would spread every artefact thinly across every phase, so no phase ever fully validates one.

distractors.A: Single management chains make change easier to lead, which is a genuine advantage and the usual reason organisations phase geographically. It is the wrong axis when the technical risk is not organised that way: each site phase would ship all the untested artefacts at once.
distractors.B: Time-zone grouping is a support-coverage convenience and does not correspond to any source of quality risk in this system. It also inherits the same defect as site phasing. Support hours are a staffing question that can be solved independently of how the rollout is sequenced.
distractors.D: Deferring localisation splits the rollout on a dimension the stem says is already solved by configuration, and it leaves non-English sites waiting on a separate programme that will need its own funding and schedule.

explanation.concept: Phase along the axis where the artefacts and the risk actually vary, not along the org chart. Identify what differs technically between candidate phases: if that is the prompt, index or tool set, phase on it; if the only difference is configuration, phasing on it buys nothing and delays validation.
explanation.tip: Find the sentence telling you which dimension is merely configuration. It is there to eliminate the organisationally natural phasing, which is otherwise the answer most people reach for.

topic: Rollback control when a third party owns the front end
stem: A retailer's Claude-based gift-card fraud explanation feature is surfaced inside a third-party contact-centre platform the retailer does not control. The vendor releases quarterly and has refused to expose a feature flag. The retailer's production readiness review asks how a bad release would be withdrawn. What should the retailer require before go-live?

options.text: A contractual commitment from the vendor to ship an emergency release within 48 hours of a written request from the retailer.
Staged enablement by contact-centre team, configured through the vendor platform's existing user management features.
A pre-release soak in the vendor's staging environment covering a full quarter of historical traffic patterns before each release.
A kill switch in the retailer's own API that returns a defined unavailable response the vendor's interface already handles.

explanation.correct: The retailer cannot change the vendor's release train, so the withdrawal mechanism must live entirely on the retailer's side of the boundary. Serving a defined unavailable response from the retailer's own API removes the feature within seconds and depends on nobody, provided the vendor interface already has a rendering path for that response — which is the detail to confirm during integration rather than during an incident. Owning the off switch at the layer you control is the general rule whenever a partner owns the presentation layer.

distractors.A: A 48-hour commitment is a promise about a future negotiation, not a control. It also leaves two days of a bad feature in front of agents and customers, which for a fraud explanation is two days of wrong explanations.
distractors.B: Staged enablement limits how many teams are exposed and does not remove the feature from those already enabled. It also depends on vendor functionality that the retailer neither controls nor can change under pressure.
distractors.C: Soak testing lowers the chance of shipping something bad and does nothing once something bad is shipped. Readiness reviews ask about withdrawal precisely because prevention is never complete. It is also carried out in an environment the retailer can neither inspect nor reproduce.

explanation.concept: Place the kill switch on the side of the integration boundary you control. When a partner owns the user interface and its release cadence, design the backend contract so a defined degraded response withdraws the feature immediately, and verify during integration that the partner's interface renders that response acceptably.
explanation.tip: Sort the options by who has to act for them to work. Anything requiring the third party to do something on your timetable is not a control you own, however firmly it is written into the contract.

topic: Agenda for the first post-implementation review
stem: A regional water utility launched a Claude-based leak-report triage assistant ninety days ago and holds its first post-implementation review next week. Which items belong on the agenda because they answer questions neither the pilot gate nor the readiness review could? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: A retrospective assessment of whether a different architectural pattern would have suited the problem better.
The model provider's published roadmap for new capabilities the utility might adopt in the next financial year, and what each of them could be worth.
Whether the benefit forecast at the pilot gate has materialised at full volume, measured the same way it was measured at the gate.
The failure modes that appeared in production and were absent from the pilot, and what has entered the regression suite as a result.
Whether the operating model is working: who has been paged, how often, and whether the run team has acted without the build team.

explanation.correct: Ninety days of production supplies three things no earlier gate could. Realised benefit against forecast corrects the business case and every business case that cites it. Production-only failure modes reveal what the pilot's population missed, and tracking whether they reached the regression suite tests the feedback loop rather than just the system. Paging data and unaided run-team actions are the first real evidence that the ownership transfer took, as opposed to having been signed off on paper.

distractors.A: Re-litigating the pattern choice is a discussion with no decision attached, since the system exists and the context has moved. If a pattern change is genuinely needed, it arrives as a backlog item from the failure data, not from a retrospective opinion.
distractors.B: Provider roadmap review is planning input for the next cycle and belongs in a separate forum. It crowds out the review's actual purpose, which is reading what happened rather than speculating about what could.

explanation.concept: A post-implementation review reads three things: realised versus forecast benefit, the production failure modes the pilot could not have found and whether they became tests, and whether the operating model held. Its outputs are a corrected benefit figure, a reprioritised backlog and any ownership gaps that remain open.
explanation.tip: Ask of each agenda item whether ninety days of production data is required to answer it. Anything answerable before launch, or only about the future, is not what this review is for.

topic: When rolling forward beats reverting a prompt
stem: A prompt change has caused a production quality regression. Under what condition is rolling forward with a corrected prompt preferable to reverting to the previous version?

options.text: When the previous version carries its own unresolved defect that the change was fixing, and the corrected prompt has passed the evaluation gate.
When the team is confident the fix is simple, since reverting a prompt always requires a full application release cycle and takes longer than shipping forward.
When the regression affects fewer users than the defect the original change was intended to fix.
When the prompt registry does not retain prior versions, leaving roll-forward as the only path available.

explanation.correct: Reverting is the default because it returns you to a state that has been observed in production. It stops being the default only when that previous state is itself known-bad, which is the case when the change was fixing something real. Even then, roll-forward is only acceptable if the corrected prompt has cleared the evaluation gate; shipping an unevaluated fix into a live regression is how one incident becomes two. Both halves of the condition have to hold.

distractors.B: Confidence in a simple fix is the feeling that precedes most compounded incidents, and the premise is wrong: a properly decoupled prompt reverts without an application release at all. If reverting genuinely requires a release, that is the defect to fix.
distractors.C: Comparing affected populations sounds rational and rests on nothing, because you do not yet know that the corrected prompt works. Choosing the smaller harm is only meaningful once the alternative has been shown to remove it.
distractors.D: A registry that cannot restore a prior version is a broken registry, and the correct response is to fix it rather than to treat the limitation as a decision rule. Meanwhile the regression continues.

explanation.concept: Default to reverting, because a previously observed state is the only state you have evidence about. Roll forward only when the previous version is known-defective and the replacement has passed the same evaluation gate a normal release would face. Never let urgency become the reason a change skips the gate.
explanation.tip: Watch for options where an emergency is used to justify bypassing evaluation. On this exam, incident pressure never removes the gate; it only changes which known state you are heading toward.

topic: Transferring run cost when pilot funding ends
stem: A media group's Claude-based archive-tagging service was built by a central innovation team on innovation funding. It is now in production serving three business units. At the first post-launch review, monthly spend is running at 3.4 times the pilot forecast, driven almost entirely by one unit's bulk re-tagging jobs. The innovation team's budget ends in two months and its engineers move to other work. Which two things must the lifecycle plan do? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Cap total monthly spend at the pilot forecast and throttle all requests once the cap is reached.
Extend the innovation team's funding for a further year while a chargeback model is designed and agreed.
Move the bulk re-tagging workload onto a cheaper model tier, chosen and applied by the central team before it disperses.
Attribute cost per business unit through request tagging and move run cost onto the consuming units' budgets, with the bulk re-tagging unit funding its own load.
Name a budget owner in each consuming unit who approves that unit's spend and receives its monthly consumption report.

explanation.correct: Ownership transfer includes financial ownership, and here the innovation budget disappears in two months. Per-unit attribution is the prerequisite: without it, nobody can be charged and the overspend has no address. A named budget owner per unit is what turns attribution into control, because a report with no recipient changes nobody's behaviour and the unit generating the bulk load currently has no reason to care what it costs. Together they place the cost decision with the party who controls the demand.

distractors.A: A global cap throttles three units for one unit's consumption, so the two well-behaved units absorb an outage they did not cause. Caps belong per consumer, and only after attribution exists to enforce them.
distractors.B: Extending central funding removes the deadline that is forcing the transfer to happen, and a year later the same conversation occurs with a larger bill and no engineers who remember the system.
distractors.C: A tier change is a plausible optimisation and it is the consuming unit's decision to make once it owns the bill. Applied centrally on the way out of the door, it changes output quality for a workload the central team no longer supports.

explanation.concept: Transfer of ownership includes cost ownership. Before the building team's funding ends, instrument per-consumer attribution, name a budget owner for each consumer, and route consumption reporting to them. Optimisation decisions then sit with whoever pays, which is the only arrangement in which they get made.
explanation.tip: When a stem gives a spend overrun concentrated in one consumer plus a funding cliff, the answer is attribution and accountability, not throttling or tuning. Look for who is able to change the behaviour driving the cost.

topic: Sponsor changing the success metric mid-pilot
stem: Four weeks into an eight-week pilot of a Claude-based tender-response drafter at a construction firm, the sponsor emails: "Let's judge this on win rate rather than drafting hours saved." The criterion agreed before the pilot was a reduction in drafting hours. Tenders submitted during the pilot will not be decided for about five months, and the firm's own analyst says the pilot's forty tenders cannot distinguish a five-point change in win rate from noise. What is the next step?

options.text: Adopt win rate as the criterion, since it sits far closer to the commercial outcome the firm ultimately cares about than an activity measure such as drafting hours ever could.
Report both measures at the readout and let the sponsor decide how to weight them when the decision is taken.
Hold the agreed criterion for the pilot decision, and separately commit to a win-rate read at five months with a stated sample size requirement.
Extend the pilot until enough tenders have been submitted and decided to measure win rate directly.

explanation.correct: The proposed criterion cannot be measured inside the pilot on two independent grounds: the outcomes arrive five months late, and forty tenders are too few to detect the effect size anyway. Switching to it would produce a decision made on a number that does not exist. Holding the agreed criterion keeps the pilot decidable, and scheduling a properly powered win-rate read as a post-implementation measure gives the sponsor the commercial question they actually want answered, at the point where it can be answered.

distractors.A: The sponsor's instinct is sound — activity measures are weak proxies for value — and that argument belonged in the design conversation eight weeks ago. Adopting an unmeasurable criterion mid-pilot converts a decidable experiment into an undecidable one.
distractors.B: Presenting both and deferring the weighting is the shape a criterion-free pilot takes. One of the two measures will not exist at the readout, so in practice this means the decision is made on impressions with numbers attached.
distractors.D: Extending until win rate is measurable means waiting at least five months and then discovering the sample was never large enough. The analyst's statement rules this out before the scheduling question arises.

explanation.concept: When a sponsor proposes a new success measure mid-pilot, test it for measurability inside the pilot window and for statistical power at pilot volume. If it fails either, keep the agreed criterion for the gate and schedule the sponsor's measure as a post-implementation read with an explicit sample requirement.
explanation.tip: Two facts kill a proposed metric: the data arrives after the decision, and the sample cannot resolve the effect. When a stem supplies both, no option that adopts or waits for that metric can be right.
